title: "Spring Cloud Bus and Refresh"
description: "A worked lesson based on the supplied Spring Cloud course."
---

**Course source:** Day 4 §2.5–§2.6. **Running example:** a shop with Product, Order and User services.

## One changed setting, many instances

Suppose Order has three replicas. A manual configuration refresh request to one replica does not guarantee that the others re-read settings. The source introduces **Spring Cloud Bus**, which uses a broker-backed event mechanism to distribute refresh notifications.

~~~text
Configuration changed
         |
  refresh notification
         v
      Message bus
      /    |     \
   Order A B      C
       reload configuration
~~~

The bus distributes a **signal**; each instance still needs to fetch and apply the current configuration appropriately. A signal can be delayed or missed, so delivery observability and reconciliation matter.

## Avoid treating updates as transactions

A distributed configuration refresh does not guarantee that every Order instance switches at one exact instant. For a period, different replicas may operate under different setting versions.

Design changes so mixed versions are safe. For example, changing a timeout from 350 ms to 400 ms is usually less risky than changing a wire protocol or removing an endpoint abruptly.

## A conceptual event

~~~json
{
  "type": "config.refresh",
  "application": "order",
  "version": "config-184"
}
~~~

This is an original illustration rather than a Spring Cloud Bus wire format.

## Security and operations

The ability to trigger fleet-wide refresh can alter production behaviour. Protect refresh endpoints, authenticate bus participants, validate config changes and audit who authorised them.

Measure delivery delay, applied version per replica and refresh failures. If all instances must converge eventually, reconcile periodically rather than relying on one broadcast alone.

## When not to refresh dynamically

Changing connection topology, TLS credentials or other complex resources may require a rolling restart instead. The convenience of refresh is subordinate to correctness.

## Questions to answer aloud

What problem does this design solve? Which guarantee does it give, and which guarantee does it **not** give? How would you detect incorrect operation?
